exercises.objective: Explain why the formal h(q,qdot,t)=0 definition and the tangent-space dim(U_x)<dim(x) definition of non-holonomic agree.
exercises.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why a constraint of the form $h(q,\dot q,t)=0$ (restricting achievable velocities) is the same idea as saying the tangent space generated by controls, $U_x=\{\dot x:\dot x=f(x,u),u\in U\}$, has $\dim(U_x)<\dim(x)$.
hints: $h(q,\dot q,t)=0$ directly says: not every $\dot q$ is achievable at a given $q$, only those satisfying the constraint equation.

$U_x$ is, by definition, exactly the set of $\dot x$ values actually achievable via some control $u$; if $U_x$ is a proper subspace of the full tangent space (dimension strictly less than $\dim(x)$), that's precisely a restriction on which velocities are achievable.

So both are saying the same thing in different notation: $h(q,\dot q,t)=0$ names the restriction as an explicit constraint equation, while $\dim(U_x)<\dim(x)$ names it as a dimension-counting fact about the set of achievable velocities; a system satisfies one iff it satisfies the other.

exercises.objective: Derive the car model's differential constraint from its equations of motion.
exercises.prompt: Given $\dot x=v\cos\theta,\ \dot y=v\sin\theta$, show that $\dot x\sin\theta-\dot y\cos\theta=0$ for any value of $v$ (the steering angle $\dot\theta$ doesn't enter this particular identity).
hints: Both terms are $v\sin\theta\cos\theta$, just written in a different order.

$v\sin\theta\cos\theta-v\sin\theta\cos\theta=0$, identically, for any $v,\theta$: the identity holds regardless of the specific control values, confirming it's a genuine constraint on the *velocity direction* (perpendicular-to-heading motion is always zero), not something that happens to hold only for particular controls. (Independently verified symbolically with SymPy while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Count dim(U_x) for the car model and confirm it is genuinely non-holonomic.
exercises.prompt: The car's state is $q=(x,y,\theta)$, so $\dim(q)=3$. Its controls are $u=(v,\phi)$: only 2 free parameters determine the achievable velocity direction at any instant (the differential constraint removes one direction from the 3D tangent space). What is $\dim(U_q)$? Enter an integer.
hints: $U_q$ is the set of achievable $\dot q=(\dot x,\dot y,\dot\theta)$ values, parameterized by the 2 free controls $(v,\phi)$.
Even though $\dot q$ lives in a 3D space, the differential constraint $\dot x\sin\theta-\dot y\cos\theta=0$ confines achievable $\dot q$ to a 2-dimensional subspace of that 3D tangent space.
$\dim(U_q)=2<\dim(q)=3$: confirms the car is non-holonomic, exactly matching the general definition.

exercises.objective: Explain why control-based sampling guarantees feasible edges where straight-line PRM/RRT can fail.
exercises.prompt: A PRM built directly in $(x,y,\theta)$ with a straight-line local planner can connect two configurations even if no sequence of car controls actually achieves that motion. Explain precisely why control-based sampling can't produce this same failure.
hints: A straight-line local planner only checks whether the geometric path between two configurations avoids obstacles; it never checks whether that path is actually achievable given the car's differential constraint, so it can 'connect' configurations that require impossible sideways motion.

Control-based sampling never proposes a path first and checks it after: it picks an actual control $u$, integrates the true equations of motion forward from the current configuration, and only then adds whatever endpoint that produces to the tree.

So every edge in a control-based-sampling tree is, by construction, exactly the result of some real, executable control sequence: there's no way to end up with an edge the car couldn't actually drive, unlike the straight-line planner which never checks achievability at all.
